1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We introduced Controlled Style Decomposition (CSD), a black-box framework yielding two findings across four judges, three benchmarks, and three style axes.
5	First, the Likert Blindspot: Likert scoring systematically misses style biases that pairwise comparison detects---complete at moderate bias ($d \to 0$ at $n = 355$), ${>}60\%$ attenuation at stronger effects---confirmed by seven statistical methods.
6	Whether this reflects measurement attenuation or construct divergence, Likert-only audits miss style-driven preferences that propagate through alignment pipelines.
7	Second, GEE conditional decomposition demonstrates per-axis confound structure consistent across three architectures---verbosity style-dominated, formality conditional, register judge-dependent---determining which estimates require conditional analysis and informing debiasing priorities.
8	
9	Pairwise comparison offers superior detection sensitivity for style bias, provided that amplification controls---position balancing, content filtering, and per-axis decomposition---are in place (\S\ref{sec:amplification}); existing Likert-based null findings may reflect measurement insensitivity rather than genuine absence of bias.
10	Our findings are established on English benchmarks with $n \leq 355$; validation on larger corpora, additional languages, and emerging judge architectures remains necessary.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{False negative rate.}
We validate all 100 NLI decisions against an LLM annotator (Qwen3-32B) prompted to judge whether semantic content is preserved.
The two systems agree on 91 of 100 pairs (Gwet's AC1 $= 0.89$; Cohen's $\kappa = 0.43$ is depressed by prevalence skew \citep{feinstein1990kappa}).
Of the 12 rejected pairs, 8 are judged content-preserving by the LLM annotator, yielding an overall false negative rate of $8/95 = 8.4\%$.
Since this annotator shares the same model (Qwen3-32B) as the rewriter, the FNR estimate may be optimistic; the independent GPT-4o cross-validation below provides model-independent verification.
Three robustness checks confirm these do not compromise conclusions: BT stable across 11 NLI thresholds from 0.50 to 0.98 (${\leq}3$pp variation across all four judge$\times$axis configurations; \S\ref{sec:nli_threshold}), no covariate differences between retained and discarded pairs (all $p > 0.12$; \S\ref{sec:consistency}), and no directional bias in false negatives (Fisher $p = 0.35$).
The NLI gate operates as a precision-oriented conservative filter (precision $= 98.9\%$); verbosity-rejected pairs have larger edit distances (Cliff's $\delta = +0.45$, $p < 0.001$), making estimates lower bounds.
Full-scale GPT-4o validation on all 200 NLI gate decisions yields 92.1\% pass precision for formality and 82.6\% for verbosity, with the lower verbosity figure reflecting the permissiveness of direction-aware gating (17.4\% false positives vs.\ 7.9\% for the strict bidirectional formality gate---a trade-off for the higher pass rate that enables adequate sample sizes).
Admitted false positives would inflate verbosity BT only if content-leaked pairs systematically favor the styled variant; the GEE originality OR ${<}1$ indicates the opposite direction, making the verbosity BT estimate a conservative lower bound on pure style preference.

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
\label{sec:nli_threshold}
A continuous sweep across 11 NLI thresholds (0.50--0.98) confirms that BT estimates are robust to threshold choice: all 44 judge$\times$axis$\times$threshold combinations are significant, with maximum variation ${\leq}3$pp within each configuration (Appendix~\ref{app:nli_sweep}).
NLI scores follow a bimodal distribution (most pairs above 0.95 or below 0.30), so the 0.90 threshold lies on a plateau rather than a cliff edge.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	LLM judges are widely deployed for evaluation and alignment, yet style features alone explain judge scores with near-perfect correlation.
3	We introduce Controlled Style Decomposition (CSD), a unified framework combining NLI-gated content control, per-axis style decomposition, and position-controlled pairwise comparison to systematically quantify style bias in LLM judges.

7	Whether this divergence reflects measurement attenuation or genuine construct divergence, both interpretations yield the same operational conclusion: Likert-only evaluation systematically misses style-driven preferences that propagate through pairwise-based alignment pipelines.

\section{Introduction}

LLM judges are central infrastructure for NLP evaluation (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena) and alignment training (RLHF, DPO), where judge-generated preferences serve as reward signals.
Any systematic bias in their assessments propagates through both evaluation leaderboards and model development pipelines.

Recent work suggests that style features alone explain most of the variance in judge scores \citep{murugadoss2025sos}, motivating systematic measurement of per-axis style bias.
\citet{li2026preference} demonstrate that 76--92\% of observed preference signals originate from surface-level style cues rather than substantive quality differences, and \citet{soumik2026judging} report bias scores of 0.76--0.92 across five different judges.
Despite this consensus on severity, existing approaches each address individual requirements: CASSE \citep{casse2026concise} and FairJudge \citep{wang2026fairjudge} provide multi-dimensional style analysis, RATE \citep{reber2025rate} introduces interventional design, and length-controlled AlpacaEval \citep{dubois2025lc} offers population-level correction.
However, no single framework integrates all four requirements---per-axis decomposition, interventional identification, per-instance diagnostics, and black-box applicability.
A further concern compounds these limitations: standard Likert scoring suffers from a measurement efficiency gap---integer discretization produces ${\sim}60\%$ uninformative ties, and even non-tied pairs carry weaker signal than pairwise comparison---a limitation predicted by measurement theory \citep{thurstone1927law} but previously unquantified for LLM judges.

We propose Controlled Style Decomposition (CSD), a unified framework combining NLI-gated content control, per-axis style decomposition, and position-controlled pairwise comparison to systematically quantify style bias in LLM judges.
Inspired by interventional approaches to text analysis \citep{veitch2020adapting}, CSD operates in three stages: binary style-controlled rewriting along a single axis (e.g., formal vs.\ casual), content preservation verification through Natural Language Inference (NLI) entailment scoring, and bias measurement via position-controlled pairwise comparison.
Because CSD requires no access to judge internals and applies post-hoc to any black-box judge, it complements existing population-level approaches with finer-grained, per-instance diagnostics.
Our experiments quantify this efficiency gap---which we term the \emph{Likert Blindspot}---across four target judges (GPT-4o, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash) and one negative control (Claude Sonnet 4), three benchmarks, and two primary style axes (formality, verbosity), with exploratory evidence on register.
On the same formality data, Likert scoring yields non-significant ATE ($p = 0.332$, $p = 0.908$) for both judges, while Bradley-Terry analysis detects 63.0\% (GPT-4o, $p = 0.0004$) and 66.5\% (Qwen3-32B, $p < 0.0001$) formal win probabilities; verbosity shows 77.3\% BT ($p < 0.0001$) invisible to Likert ($p = 0.179$; Figure~\ref{fig:forest_plot}).

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{A black-box controlled framework} for detecting per-axis style bias in LLM judges through style-controlled rewriting and position-controlled pairwise comparison (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
    \item \textbf{The Likert Blindspot:} Likert scoring systematically misses style biases that pairwise comparison detects, following a severity spectrum---complete at moderate bias ($d \to 0$ at $n = 355$), ${>}60\%$ attenuation at stronger effects---across six judge$\times$axis configurations ($p < 0.001$ pairwise vs.\ $p > 0.17$ Likert). Whether this reflects measurement attenuation or construct divergence, the operational consequence is identical; seven statistical methods confirm the effect is structural (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}, Tables~\ref{tab:main_results}--\ref{tab:sensitivity}).
    \item \textbf{Per-axis confound structure:} GEE conditional decomposition demonstrates that verbosity bias is style-dominated across all four target judges (Style OR $8$--$13$, Orig OR ${<}1$), formality is conditional (significant style and originality effects), and register is judge-dependent (originality-dominated to mixed)---this structure determines which CSD estimates are directly interpretable (verbosity) versus requiring conditional interpretation (formality), and is invisible to aggregate metrics (Section~\ref{sec:direction}, Table~\ref{tab:gee}).
    \item \textbf{Practical implications:} style bias audits require pairwise comparison \emph{and} per-axis decomposition; aggregate metrics and Likert-based findings may systematically underestimate bias or conflate distinct confound structures (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\end{itemize}
